title: Zero-source LLM Hallucination Detection with Human-like Criteria Probing
claim: An agent decomposes judgment into weighted criteria, scores and aggregates them, and is trained with a reward, mirroring human multi-criteria evaluation.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, human criteria left, mechanism right with feedback loop
description: A two-part diagram split by a vertical line. The left panel, titled 'Human Judgement', shows six rounded green boxes (Logical Consistency, Factual Verification, Semantic Accuracy, Social Fairness, Timeline Verification) around a cartoon of a thinking person with question marks. The right panel, 'Human-like Criteria Probing Mechanism', starts with a Q&A box feeding an AI robot icon labeled Agent f_θ. Blue arrows labeled 'Multi Sampling' and red arrows labeled 'Rolling Out' lead into a light-blue region. That region holds stacked boxes of '<Criteria c_i: (Weight w_i)>' paired with red-dashed '<Analysis><Score s_p^(k)>' boxes. Blue arrows lead on to an 'Aggregate' step and a Final Score [s̄/10] box. A red arrow goes from the last score to a pink Reward Function box, then a long red 'Online Update' arrow returns to the agent. A legend at top right marks blue as Inference and red as GRPO.
caption: Overview of the proposed HCPD. Given a query–answer pair $(q, a)$, the agent instantiates a set of specific criteria $\{c_i\}_{i=1}^m$ and corresponding importance weights $\{w_i\}_{i=1}^m$. The criterion-level partial scores $\{s_i\}_{i=1}^m$ are subsequently produced and aggregated into an overall truthfulness measure $s_p$. During GRPO training, we fine-tune the agent by maximizing the score-alignment reward that encourages the predicted $s_p$ to match weak supervision labels derived from consistency-based similarity measures. At inference time, we invoke the agent $K$ times and aggregate the resulting scores to obtain a reliable decision $\bar{s}$.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often hallucinate by generating factually incorrect or unfaithful content, posing significant risks to their safe use. Detecting such hallucinations is particularly challenging under the zero-source constraint, where no model internals or external references are available, and detection must rely solely on the textual query-answer pair. In this paper, we propose Human-like Criteria Probing for Hallucination Detection (HCPD), a paradigm that emulates the multi-faceted reasoning of human evaluators. Its core is a Human-like Criteria Probing (HCP) mechanism, in which a LLM agent adaptively decomposes its judgment into a weighted set of interpretable criteria and aggregates criterion-specific scores into a final truthfulness measure. To achieve this adaptive capability, we introduce a reward-based alignment scheme using only weak supervision from semantic consistency. At inference, we employ a multi-sampling aggregation strategy to ensure robust decisions while preserving full interpretability. We further provide theoretical analysis supporting the reliability of our approach. Extensive experiments show that HCPD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, offering an effective and explainable solution for zero-source hallucination detection. Code is available at https://github.com/TRISKEL10N/HCPD.
